blocks.heading: What this section covers
blocks.text: Organise the analysis around the text’s purpose and effect, not the order of its paragraphs; write it in a formal, precise analytical register.

blocks.heading: Organising by effect
blocks.text: An analysis organised by effect or purpose builds an argument about the whole text; one that follows the order of the text’s paragraphs tends to become a commentary on each in turn. The plan is made before writing: decide the two or three things the text does to its reader, give each a section that gathers evidence from wherever it occurs, and let the introduction state the view and the conclusion gather it.

blocks.heading: The analytical register
blocks.text: The analytical register is formal and precise: third person, present tense, exact terms, embedded quotations, no chatty asides. "The writer personifies the fog as a visitor" is in the register; "I think this bit is really clever" is a conversational commentary, and it weakens the analysis because it argues nothing — the register is the argument’s clothing, and chatty dress makes the reader expect a chat.

blocks.heading: Worked example: a plan made before writing
blocks.text: From a charity leaflet, planned by effect rather than paragraph order: first, the leaflet makes the reader feel the drought ("walks into every village at once"); second, it makes the solution feel easy ("that is not charity; that is infrastructure"); third, it makes giving feel immediate ("Do it now, while the dry season is doing its worst"). Three effects, one section each, evidence gathered from across the text — and the walkthrough trap is avoided because the plan never once asked "what happens in paragraph two?"

blocks.heading: In the exam
blocks.text: The text analysis is Section B of Paper 1: twenty-five marks, five for reading and twenty for analysis, opened by the instruction Analyse and set on an unseen text of about 550–750 words. Two hours and fifteen minutes cover both sections, so the analysis gets its share of the time — and the strongest answers spend two minutes of that on the plan, because a plan by effect saves the ten minutes a walkthrough costs when its paragraphs need rebuilding. Write the opening, make the plan, then write to it: form, audience, purpose and effect in a sentence; two or three sections argued by evidence from across the text; a conclusion that gathers.

blocks.heading: One toolkit, three tasks
blocks.text: Everything taught here works on the other analysis questions too: the comparison of Paper 1 Question 1(b) is this analysis done to two texts, with the connectives added; the reflective commentary of Paper 2 is this analysis done to your own writing, with the brief in place of the context. Learn feature, evidence, effect, link once, and the whole AO3 share of the qualification — forty of the hundred marks — is one skill wearing three different briefs. The organisation by effect and the analytical register travel with it, and the misconceptions filed here — summary, spot-naming, the walkthrough — are the same errors the other tasks record, which is why this topic’s habits are worth more than its marks: they are the whole qualification’s habits, learned once, in the place with the most room to practise them.

blocks.heading: The walkthrough
blocks.text: Working through the text paragraph by paragraph, or jumping around it with no line of argument, scatters the analysis: points about the same effect end up far apart, and the answer never states a view of the text. The test is to read the first sentence of each paragraph in turn — together they should state an argument about the whole text, not a route through it. The fix is the plan by effect, made before writing, and the paragraphs follow the plan instead of the source’s order.
